## Goal

Distinguish precision, bias, reading SD, uncertainty in a mean and uncertainty in
a derived analytical result. Calculate a small independent-input budget and
explain why shared effects do not disappear when readings are repeated.

## Background

Repeated readings of one stable preparation can reveal **reading repeatability**.
They do not by themselves reveal sampling, extraction loss, stock uncertainty or
shared volume effects. For independent normal readings, $s/\sqrt n$ estimates the
reading contribution to uncertainty in their mean. Standard uncertainty is on
an SD-like scale; it is not automatically a 95% half-width.

For $c=c_sV_a/V_f$ and small independent input uncertainties,

$$u(c)=c\sqrt{[u(c_s)/c_s]^2+[u(V_a)/V_a]^2+[u(V_f)/V_f]^2}.$$

Correlated inputs require covariance terms. A known significant bias calls for
investigation or a justified correction with its uncertainty, rather than an
arbitrary extra error bar.

## By hand

**B1.** A reference is 10.00 mg/L. Method A has mean 10.00 and SD 0.02 mg/L;
B has mean 10.50 and the same SD. Compare precision and estimated bias. Here
reference uncertainty is neglected. [Hint](#hint-b1)

**B2.** Five independent stable readings have mean 10.00 and SD 0.3162 mg/L.
Calculate the reading uncertainty in the mean. Which quantity still has SD
0.3162 mg/L? [Hint](#hint-b2)

**B3.** A 100.0 mg/L stock has standard uncertainty 0.4 mg/L. A 5.000 mL aliquot
has standard uncertainty 0.006 mL; final volume 50.00 mL has standard uncertainty
0.03 mL. Calculate final concentration, each output-scale contribution and their
combined standard uncertainty. [Hint](#hint-b3)

**B4.** Reading noise contributes $0.20/\sqrt n$ mg/L and an independent shared
component is 0.10 mg/L. Find combined uncertainty at $n=1$ and $n=100$, and its
limit as n grows. [Hint](#hint-b4)

**B5.** A report gives “10.00 ± 0.04 mg/L” without defining ±. Name two possible
meanings and the information needed to distinguish them. [Hint](#hint-b5)

## In R

Run from the supplied project root. The reference-material table contains
repeat readings of one material by each method, not independent collected waters.

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
measurements <- read_csv("data/course/precision.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
summary_precision <- measurements |>
  group_by(method) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_mg_l = mean(measured_mg_l),
            sd_mg_l = sd(measured_mg_l),
            u_mean_mg_l = sd_mg_l / sqrt(n),
            bias_mg_l = mean_mg_l - first(reference_mg_l), .groups = "drop")
summary_precision
ggplot(measurements, aes(measured_mg_l, method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 10, linetype = "dashed") + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Measured concentration (mg/L)", y = "Method") + theme_minimal()
c_final <- 100 * 5 / 50
contributions <- c(stock = c_final * .4 / 100,
                   aliquot = c_final * .006 / 5,
                   final = c_final * .03 / 50)
u_c <- sqrt(sum(contributions^2))
c(concentration_mg_l = c_final, standard_uncertainty_mg_l = u_c)
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(summary_precision, "output/precision-summary.csv")
write_csv(data.frame(source = names(contributions),
                    u_mg_l = as.numeric(contributions)), "output/dilution-budget.csv")
```

**R1.** Identify the precise but displaced method. Compare A/B's reading SD
with C's. Does C's mean matching the reference establish an unbiased method
across matrices? [Hint](#hint-r1)

**R2.** Confirm B3. Halve only the stock standard uncertainty to 0.2 mg/L and
recompute. Why does combined uncertainty not halve exactly? [Hint](#hint-r2)

**R3.** Draw B4's curve in R. Explain which source would remain after infinitely
many readings. State whether this includes a deliberately uncorrected known
bias. [Hint](#hint-r3)

```r
n <- 1:100
u_reading <- .20 / sqrt(n)
u_combined <- sqrt(u_reading^2 + .10^2)
plot(n, u_combined, type = "l", xlab = "Readings of one preparation",
     ylab = "Standard uncertainty of mean (mg/L)")
lines(n, u_reading, lty = 2)
abline(h = .10, lty = 3)
```

**R4.** Export `repeat-readings-and-uncertainty.csv`, save it at the project root,
and compare its observed reading SD with its supplied model uncertainty:

```r
if (file.exists("repeat-readings-and-uncertainty.csv")) {
  demo <- read_csv("repeat-readings-and-uncertainty.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
  print(mean(demo$reported_reading_mg_l))
  if (nrow(demo) > 1) print(sd(demo$reported_reading_mg_l))
  print(unique(demo$mean_standard_uncertainty_model_mg_l))
}
```

Why are the last two numbers different quantities? [Hint](#hint-r4)

## Hints

::: {#hint-b1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B1"}
Precision concerns repeated values; estimated bias compares mean with a suitable
reference. They answer different questions.
:::

::: {#hint-b2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B2"}
Divide SD by $\sqrt5$ for the reading contribution to the mean. The individual
reading distribution retains its own spread.
:::

::: {#hint-b3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B3"}
Final concentration is 10 mg/L. Convert each relative input uncertainty to an
output-scale contribution before adding its square.
:::

::: {#hint-b4 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B4"}
Combine the squared reading and shared components. Only the independent reading
term is divided by n.
:::

::: {#hint-b5 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B5"}
It could denote a standard uncertainty, expanded uncertainty with a stated
coverage factor, or a confidence-interval half-width under a sampling model.
:::

::: {#hint-explore .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hints E1–E4"}
Track reading noise, common random offset and deliberately known fixed bias
separately. The bias correction is exact only by this toy model's assumption;
real corrections can have their own uncertainty.
:::

::: {#hint-r1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R1"}
Compare both `bias_mg_l` and `sd_mg_l`. A single accidentally close mean is not
full validation.
:::

::: {#hint-r2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R2"}
Change only the stock contribution from 0.040 to 0.020 mg/L. Keep the two volume
contributions.
:::

::: {#hint-r3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R3"}
[`sqrt()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/MathFun.html)
is applied to the sum of variances. A known uncorrected bias is not being treated
as an extra random term in this illustrative curve.
:::

::: {#hint-r4 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R4"}
[`sd()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/sd.html)
describes spread among readings. The supplied uncertainty includes a component
shared by those readings, which their scatter cannot estimate.
:::

## Solutions

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions B1–B5"}
**B1.** A and B have equal repeat precision under the stated conditions. A has
estimated bias zero in this series; B has +0.50 mg/L. Equal precision does not
imply equal closeness to the reference, and this neglects reference uncertainty
only for the example.

**B2.** $u_{reading}(\bar x)=0.3162/\sqrt5\approx0.1414$ mg/L. Individual
readings retain SD 0.3162 mg/L; the mean has a smaller reading component. Neither
number establishes sampling, recovery or common-bias uncertainty.

**B3.** $c=100(5/50)=10$ mg/L. Contributions are 0.040, 0.012 and 0.006 mg/L.
Their squared sum is 0.001780 (mg/L)², so $u(c)=0.04219$ mg/L. The calculation
assumes a valid model, small uncertainties and independent inputs.

**B4.** At n=1, $u=\sqrt{0.20^2+0.10^2}=0.22361$ mg/L. At n=100,
$u=\sqrt{0.20^2/100+0.10^2}=0.10198$ mg/L. It approaches 0.10 mg/L, because
repeated readings do not create new information about the common effect.

**B5.** If 0.04 is a standard uncertainty, no 95% coverage is implied by itself.
If it is expanded uncertainty, give k and its coverage rationale. If it is a
confidence-interval half-width, give the sampling/model construction and level.
Without that information the reader cannot interpret the uncertainty claim.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions E1–E4"}
**E1.** The reading-only component is 0.20, 0.06325 and 0.0200 mg/L at n=1,10,100;
combined values are about 0.22361, 0.11832 and 0.10198 mg/L. The mean can remain
displaced because bias and the common offset do not shrink within the run.

**E2.** The readings coincide and their observed SD is zero for n≥2. The known
bias and realised shared offset remain. Zero observed repeatability scatter
therefore does not establish an exact analytical result.

**E3.** Subtracting the specified known bias removes the fixed 0.30 mg/L effect.
The common random offset remains, along with residual reading noise. The model
assumes the correction exact; a real correction may add an uncertainty component.

**E4.** A new run draws a new common offset. Many readings within one preparation
retain the same offset. Studying independent preparations can reveal sources
that within-solution repeatability cannot, provided the design actually varies
the relevant steps.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions R1–R4"}
**R1.** B is precise but displaced. A/B both have SD about 0.01581 mg/L; C has
SD 0.31623 mg/L. C's mean is 10.00 in this small series, but that does not prove
unbiased performance in different samples, matrices or conditions.

**R2.** New combined uncertainty is $\sqrt{0.020^2+0.012^2+0.006^2}=0.02408$
mg/L. The unchanged volume terms prevent a simple factor-of-two change.

**R3.** The shared 0.10 mg/L component remains. The curve omits a known
uncorrected bias rather than pretending it is random; that bias requires its
own investigation or justified correction. The values are standard uncertainties,
not 95% interval half-widths.

**R4.** R's SD measures within-run reading spread and may differ from the supplied
population reading SD in a finite sample. The model uncertainty concerns the
mean and combines a shrinking independent reading contribution with a shared
component. Changing a common offset moves all readings together without widening
their scatter. At n=1, sample SD is undefined, not evidence of no variability.
:::

## Where this leads

[Calibration and quality control](../calibration-qc/exercise.qmd) adds uncertain
slope and intercept when a response is converted to concentration. Ask which
uncertainty components and validity checks accompany every later reported result.
